name: Vector_2

functions.name: texp
functions.body: if numberp(x) and x<0 then concat("\\left(",tex1(x),"\\right)") else tex1(x)

functions.name: texsumf
functions.body: block([L:first(args(e))], concat(tex1(first(L)), apply(sconcat, map(lambda([t], concat("+",texp(t))), rest(L)))))

functions.name: texnsum
functions.body: block([L:first(args(e))], concat(tex1(first(L)), apply(sconcat, map(lambda([t], if numberp(t) and t<0 then concat("-",tex1(-t)) else concat("+",tex1(t))), rest(L)))))

functions.name: cft
functions.body: concat(if c<0 then "-" else (if fst then "" else "+"), if abs(c)=1 then "" else tex1(abs(c)), tex1(s))

functions.name: texlin
functions.body: block([L:args(e), out:"", f:true], for k:1 thru length(L) step 2 do (if L[k]#0 then (out:concat(out, cft(L[k],L[k+1],f)), f:false)), if out="" then "0" else out)

questiontext:
Let \({\bf v_{1}}\), \({\bf v_2}\), \({\bf v_3}\) be the following vectors:

\[ {\bf v_{1}} = {{CT:0}},\quad {\bf v_{2}} = {{CT:1}},\quad {\bf v_{3}} = {{CT:2}}. \]

Find the values for \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) such that

\[{\bf v_3} = \lambda_1 {\bf v_1} + \lambda_2 {\bf v_2} .\]

If such values do not exist, enter zero for both entries.

\(\lambda_1\) = [[input:ans1]]      \(\lambda_2\) = [[input:ans2]]
[[validation:ans1]] [[validation:ans2]]
generalfeedback:
Outline: Comparing the components of both sides gives a linear system of two equations in \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2\). Its determinant is not zero, so it has a unique solution, which we find by Cramer's rule.
Step 1 — The linear system
If \({\bf v_3} = \lambda_{1} {\bf v_1} + \lambda_{2} {\bf v_2}\), then each component of \({\bf v_3}\) equals the same combination of the components of \({\bf v_1}\) and \({\bf v_2}\):

\[ \begin{cases} {{CT:3}}={{CT:4}} \\ {{CT:5}}={{CT:6}} \end{cases} \]

Step 2 — The determinant of the system
The columns of the coefficient matrix are \({\bf v_1}\) and \({\bf v_2}\):

\[ D=\begin{vmatrix} {{CT:7}} & {{CT:8}} \\ {{CT:9}} & {{CT:10}} \end{vmatrix}={{CT:11}}-{{CT:12}}={{CT:13}}={{CT:14}} \]

Since \(D\neq 0\), the system has exactly one solution (so such values do exist).
Step 3 — Cramer's rule
Replace the column of the unknown by the right-hand side, and divide by \(D\):

\[ \lambda_1=\frac{1}{D}\begin{vmatrix} {{CT:4}} & {{CT:8}} \\ {{CT:6}} & {{CT:10}} \end{vmatrix}=\frac{{{CT:15}}-{{CT:16}}}{ {{CT:14}} }=\frac{ {{CT:17}} }{ {{CT:14}} }={{CT:18}} \]

\[ \lambda_2=\frac{1}{D}\begin{vmatrix} {{CT:7}} & {{CT:4}} \\ {{CT:9}} & {{CT:6}} \end{vmatrix}=\frac{{{CT:19}}-{{CT:20}}}{ {{CT:14}} }=\frac{ {{CT:21}} }{ {{CT:14}} }={{CT:22}} \]

Hence

\[ \lambda_1 = {{CT:18}} ,\qquad \lambda_2 = {{CT:22}} \]
